details:
**The eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg watch over the Valley of Ashes.**
This clue references a sprawling, decaying industrial area located between West Egg and New York City, featuring a faded billboard of a pair of eyes belonging to a noted oculist named T.J. Eckleburg. The eyes are a recurring motif in the novel, often interpreted as a representation of God’s watchful eye over the moral decay and spiritual emptiness of the 1920s society depicted by F. Scott Fitzgerald.

**The green light at the end of Daisy Buchanan’s dock.**
In the novel’s final scene, Gatsby gazes at a green light situated on the dock of the Buchanans’ house in East Egg. This light serves as the novel’s central symbol, representing Gatsby’s hopes, dreams, and the "orgastic future" that perpetually recedes before him, as well as his unattainable love for Daisy.

**Nick Carraway is the narrator set in the Jazz Age.**
The novel is written as a first-person account by Nick Carraway, a Yale graduate who moves to West Egg to rent a small house next to Jay Gatsby. Carraway observes the extravagant lifestyles and moral disintegration of the characters in New York and Long Island during the 1920s, providing the central perspective through which the story is filtered.

**F. Scott Fitzgerald is the author of this novel.**
While this is a basic fact, it is the most common and definitive identifier for the work. F. Scott Fitzgerald, a leading writer of the Jazz Age, published the novel in 1925. Questions frequently pair this author name with specific plot points or symbols to identify the book.

**Myrtle Wilson is run over by a car driven by Daisy Buchanan.**
This is the climantic event of the novel. Daisy, while drunk and driving Gatsby’s yellow Rolls-Royce, hits and kills Myrtle Wilson in the Valley of Ashes. Gatsby subsequently takes the blame for the accident to protect Daisy, leading to his eventual downfall.

**Meyer Wolfsheim wears cufflinks made of human teeth.**
Meyer Wolfsheim is a mysterious bootlegger and fixer who is an early associate of Gatsby. He is famously described wearing a string of beads and cufflinks made of human molars. He is heavily implied to be the figure responsible for fixing the 1919 World Series (the Black Sox Scandal), embodying the criminal underbelly of the Jazz Age wealth.

**The phrase "boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."**
This is the concluding line of the novel, reflecting on the nature of time and the impossibility of recapturing the past. The narrator reflects on how human efforts are constantly thwarted by the relentless flow of time, encapsulating the tragic theme of the story.

**Jay Gatsby is shot by George Wilson in his swimming pool.**
After Gatsby takes the blame for Myrtle’s death, her husband, George Wilson, becomes convinced that Gatsby was also having an affair with Myrtle and owns the car that killed her. Wilson locates Gatsby at his mansion in West Egg waits for him to come out of the pool, then shoots him dead before turning the gun on himself.

**The "GENERAL RESOLVES" list written in a copy of Hopalong Cassidy.**
To illustrate the artificiality of Gatsby’s new persona, his bootlegging racket, and his self-invention, Gatsby reveals to Nick that he wrote a list of personal goals and standards ("General Resolves") in a worn copy of the adventure novel *Hopalong Cassidy* by Morgan Robertson. This act highlights his "Platonic conception" of himself.

**Owl Eyes calls Gatsby a "regular Belasco" because the books in his library are real.**
In a famous scene, a mysterious guest in soft-rimmed spectacles, known as "Owl Eyes," is amazed to discover that the thousands of books in Gatsby’s library are genuine hardcovers rather than cardboard replicas painted to look like books. He declares Gatsby to be a "regular Belasco," referring to David Belasco, a famous theater director known for lavish productions.

**Gatsby rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht in a storm on Lake Superior.**
This clue references Gatsby’s origin story, which he reveals to Nick after Gatsby is wounded. Young James Gatz, inspired by the millionaire Dan Cody, rowed out onto the lake during a storm to save Cody’s yacht. Cody later adopted Gatz as an apprentice and partner, teaching him how to become wealthy, though Gatsby eventually left him.

**Gatsby frequently addresses people as "old sport."**
The phrase "old sport" is Gatsby’s signature verbal tic, which he uses to address virtually everyone he meets. This colloquialism is a key part of his constructed persona, designed to sound sophisticated and aristocratic, though it often comes across as stilted or affected to the other characters.

**Gatsby dropped out of St. Olaf’s College and attended Oxford for five months.**
When asked about his education, Gatsby claims to have gone to Oxford for five months after the war, but he admits to Nick that he was actually a dropout from St. Olaf’s University in Minnesota. This discrepancy is part of the "mysterious" background Gatsby cultivates to hide his humble origins as a farm boy.

**Gatsby’s mansion is described as an "imitation of some Hotel de Ville in Normandy."**
Nick Carraway, who lives next door, notes that Gatsby’s house in West Egg is a "fascinating" and "colossal" edifice. Despite its size and opulence, Nick describes it as an "uncouth" imitation of a Norman villa, lacking a church nearby, which underscores Gatsby’s ambition and the artificial nature of his wealth.

**Gatsby is obsessed with the "Platonic conception" of himself.**
Nick concludes that Gatsby "sprang from his own Platonic conception of himself." This means Gatsby created his own identity and history, reinventing himself from James Gatz, a poor farm boy, into "Jay Gatsby," the wealthy gentleman, rather than being shaped by external circumstances or social conventions.
